boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Blackburn's Ford record (July 18, 1861) in Manassas Campaign [July 1861]. McDowell's July 16-17 advance, the Confederate withdrawal behind Bull Run and the demonstration at Mitchell's Ford are context. Campaign-wide movements, reinforcements, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Brigades; the live field reads 57,000 (US 35,000; CS 22,000), figures that match the NPS description's army totals. Beauregard says Tyler pushed a column of over three thousand infantry against not more than twelve hundred bayonets under Longstreet, whose brigade covered the ford with three Virginia regiments and two guns. Nicolay puts Beauregard's army at over twenty thousand along the fords, Longstreet's brigade at five regiments, and says Tyler's reconnaissance began with a squadron and two companies and grew to Richardson's brigade and a reserve brigade.
claims.rationale: The live totals are whole-army figures, not the forces at the ford; the report and history differ on Longstreet's regiments. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Beauregard describes Bull Run as a small, usually low stream with rocky, steep banks and many fords; at Blackburn's Ford the northern bank rose at least fifty feet and formed a natural parapet for the attackers, while the southern shore was almost a plain; and on July 18 not one yard of intrenchment sheltered his men there. Nicolay says Tyler could see the valley from the hill at Centreville.
claims.rationale: Ground from an interested report and a history; no map inspected. The absence of works is Beauregard's own statement.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Brigadier General P.G.T. Beauregard and Brigadier General Irvin McDowell; the live page gives McDowell as Major General. Beauregard says Longstreet immediately commanded the troops engaged and that Early brought his brigade in; Nicolay says Tyler, a division commander, went beyond his instructions and later withdrew, and that McDowell ordered all divisions forward on hearing the cannonade.
claims.rationale: Neither listed commander directed the fighting at the ford in the inspected passages; they receive no automatic credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory; NPS says McDowell was repulsed and afterwards chose a flanking movement. Beauregard says the enemy was baffled and could not force a passage, which led him into the flank movement of July 21. Nicolay calls the battle undecisive, with loss, damage and demoralization equal on both sides, while noting its effect on both commanders.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live casualty fields read 151 (US 83; CS 68). Beauregard gives his loss as 68 killed and wounded, 15 of them killed (including two missing) and 53 wounded, and says 64 enemy dead were buried and at least 20 prisoners taken. Nicolay says some sixty Union men had fallen and gives the Confederate loss as 63 killed and wounded.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Beauregard's report covers the whole July 18 action, including the Mitchell's Ford demonstration.

open_questions: Tyler's and Richardson's reports (Nos. 3-4), McDowell's July 16-20 report (No. 1), Jordan's, Longstreet's, Early's and the Washington Artillery reports (Nos. 65-79) remain deferred. NPS and the frozen description date the Union march 'On 16 July, 1862'; the inspected sources place it in 1861.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. John G. Nicolay's The Outbreak of Rebellion (Scribner, 1881) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, largely from the Official War Records for 1861; it quotes McDowell's and Johnston's reports and uses Beauregard's, and is not independent of the report families. Beauregard's July 17 telegram and his report on the July 18 engagement, dated August 1861 with the day blank (Official Records Series I, Volume II), are one family of interested Confederate accounts; the same author has the registered Shiloh group or-beauregard. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
